raw_response.country: South Africa (illustrative case discussion; also global narrative overview)

criterion_notes.c1: Examines household drinking-water service access (explicitly focusing on water rather than sanitation, p. 954), including municipal provision to informal settlements and townships, free basic water allowances, disconnections, and flow restriction in Durban, South Africa.
criterion_notes.c2: Passes BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording (yes), it examines water governance, privatisation, commercialisation, and post-apartheid municipal water policy. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (yes), the Durban discussion addresses concrete rule-type mechanisms governing household access: Free Basic Water volumetric allowances (200 and later 300 litres/day), progressive block tariffs, cost-recovery enforcement through disconnection for non-payment, debt-suspension agreements conditional on installing flow-limiting devices (orifice valves), bulk-water commercialisation (Umgeni Water), and litigation under the 1997 Water Services Act. Exclusion is driven by Criterion 3 (no empirical evidence/methods), so both decision and plain_criterion2_decision are exclude.
criterion_notes.c3: Fails Criterion 3 (E05). This article is a conceptual and narrative review essay rather than an empirical study with identifiable data/methods or a systematic empirical synthesis. The first half narratively reviews UN reports and political ecology scholarship; the second half summarises policy history and arguments drawn from secondary sources and the author's previously published Durban research (referring readers in endnote 27 to prior 2004-2008 articles for elaboration) in order to propose a Gramscian and feminist theoretical agenda, with no primary data, fieldwork methods, interviews, archival methodology, or systematic review protocol reported.
criterion_notes.c4: In its illustrative narrative on Durban, the paper mentions access-relevant outcomes including household disconnections (4000 per week in 2002-2003), severe volume restriction from orifice valves (down to 2000 litres/month), and rising household water bills, though these are cited descriptively without empirical data collection or analysis in this paper.
criterion_notes.c5: No empirical study design, data collection procedures, sampling strategy, or analytic sample are reported; the paper is a theoretical and narrative overview essay.

evidence_quotes.quote: This paper provides an overview of recent work on the political ecology of water as well as mobilising a series of case studies from the author’s own research in Durban, South Africa.
Because of this, in 1997 the municipality opted to provide drinking water free of charge, a year later, in 1998, extending this daily allowance of 200 litres to all households in the municipality.
Between 2002 and 2003 the municipality was carrying out a staggering 4000 household disconnections per week.

Thus, much of the blame for the vicious regulation of domestic water supplies in Durban must be placed squarely on the increases in bulk-water costs, themselves a direct outcome of the commercialisation of Durban’s bulk-water supplier.
In rethinking political ecologies of water by engaging the work of Antonio Gramsci, we are provided with new resources for developing a critique of everyday environments.

raw_response.exposure: Municipal Free Basic Water policy, progressive block tariffs, non-payment disconnections, flow-limiting devices, and bulk-water supplier commercialisation (discussed narratively)
raw_response.outcome: Household water disconnections, restricted water supply volumes, and tariff affordability (discussed narratively from secondary and prior published sources)
raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). Although the essay discusses household drinking-water access and rule-type tariff, disconnection, flow-limiter, and Free Basic Water mechanisms in Durban, South Africa (satisfying Criteria 1 and 2 under both plain and narrow readings), it is a theoretical and narrative literature overview essay with no empirical methodology, no identifiable study design or sample, no primary data presented, and no systematic review methods (directing readers in endnote 27 to the author's prior empirical publications for elaboration).
raw_response.study_design: Narrative literature review and theoretical essay (non-empirical)
